name: Southern Plains heat–flood–freeze
type: Stalled front: flash flood, snow, freeze
region: Oklahoma, West Texas, the Rockies, eastern US
as_of: 23 Oct 2026 (event window closed with the expiry of the Canadian and North Canadian river flood warnings, 19–20 Oct)
headline: Record heat, then record moisture, then a hard freeze within a week. A front stalled across Oklahoma between two weather systems and storms trained over the same counties, dropping 4–11 in of rain and pushing the Canadian River into major flood.
numbers: 3–6 in OKC; 4–11 in by radar west; about 9–10 in in the southern part of Kingfisher County toward Okarche, 4.5–6 in in the west (county emergency manager Randy Poindexter, KOKH, 15 Oct)
PW 2.23 in at Norman, highest October value
Canadian R. near Bridgeport 18.0 ft at 1:45 pm CDT on 14 Oct (flood stage 14 ft; NWS Norman warning, as reported by Air Sports Net)
timeline: Record late heat: Omaha four 90 °F days, Oklahoma City record highs. Ground hard after drought.
A cold front reaches Oklahoma and stalls; an upper low drops into the Four Corners while a ridge holds over the Southeast.

Training storms over central and western Oklahoma: 3–6 in in Oklahoma City, 4–11 in by radar in Canadian, Kingfisher, Blaine and Caddo counties. Norman sounding: precipitable water 2.23 in (56.6 mm), the highest October value on record. WPC Moderate Risk.

At 1:45 pm CDT on 14 October the Canadian River near Bridgeport was at 18.0 ft, above the 14.0 ft flood stage; major flooding (NWS Norman warning, as reported by Air Sports Net): an observation at that time, not the crest.
Heavy rain shifts to West Texas (roads turned to rivers); flood watches across Oklahoma and north Texas.
A Canadian high shoves the front south after dark: temperatures fall 20–25 °F, snow in the Rockies, first freeze on the High Plains.
Rivers stay high: flood warnings on the Canadian and North Canadian until 19–20 Oct.

sections.The setup: Record-warm air lingered over the Plains into mid-October, the Gulf of Mexico was unusually warm, and tropical moisture streamed north from Hurricane Simon in the eastern Pacific. Warm air holds about 7% more water vapour per °C, so the column over Oklahoma was loaded: the 2.23 in of precipitable water at Norman broke the October record.
sections.The trigger: A cold front arrived and then stopped moving. It sat between a slow upper low over the Four Corners to the west and a stubborn ridge over the Southeast to the east, so nothing pushed it on. A 45 mph low-level jet fed moist air into the front all night.
sections.What amplified it: Training: new storms kept forming at the same spot on the front and moving over the same counties, like train cars over one track. Ground baked hard by drought shed water instead of absorbing it, and urban Oklahoma City sent runoff straight into creeks.
sections.What steered it: The front stayed put because the two systems either side were blocked. It finally moved when a strong Canadian high pressed south on 15–16 October, sweeping cold air in behind it.
sections.How it ended: The cold air behind the front cut off the moisture: rain ended within a day, replaced by a 20–25 °F drop, Rocky Mountain snow and the first freeze. River flooding continues for several days as water drains downstream.
sections.Climate signal: No study. Physical reasoning: more water vapour in a warmer atmosphere raises extreme rainfall totals. The El Niño link is indirect, through moisture from Hurricane Simon.
sections.Still open: Final rain totals and peak river crests; deaths (one possible drowning not confirmed).
